answer.observations: E0 default run: tcp_goodput_bps=668859002, udp_loss_frac=0.000739, l1_util=1.0, l1_drops=492, tcp_retrans=294. The link is reported saturated, while UDP is a constant 300 Mbps flow. If UDP loss is allowed to rise only to 0.01, at most about 3 Mbps of UDP link bits can be freed, and the default TCP retransmission count is small (294 segments over 10 s, roughly a few tenths of a Mbps of payload). Therefore the most important unexplained thing is whether the apparent shortfall of TCP goodput from a simple 1 Gbps minus UDP calculation is caused by TCP loss/backoff/queue/algorithm choices, or whether it is already bounded by link capacity, packet overhead, and the UDP-loss constraint.

whys.result: Default Cubic gives 668.859 Mbps TCP goodput with 492 link drops and 294 TCP retransmissions.
whys.guess: Cubic's loss-based congestion control backs off after queue drops, so useful TCP throughput is slightly below the capacity that the saturated link could otherwise carry.
whys.unseen: The time series of cwnd, queue occupancy, and drop timing would show whether TCP repeatedly reduces its window after short queue-full periods.
whys.matters: If loss-induced backoff is the cause, a setting that reduces loss or a less loss-sensitive TCP could raise tcp_goodput_bps.
whys.reason: This makes a direct prediction that can be tested by changing tcp.type and queue length.

whys.result: The default queue length is 100 packets and the run has non-zero drops.
whys.guess: The default queue length may be limiting TCP throughput; changing it, especially making it larger, could reduce TCP loss/backoff and increase TCP goodput, while making it smaller could also change loss behavior.
whys.unseen: The standing queue and the fraction of time the queue is full are not visible from the summary metrics.
whys.matters: If queue length controls loss/backoff, l1.queue.length could be a useful knob for maximizing TCP goodput under the UDP-loss constraint.
whys.reason: Queue length is one of the two allowed knobs and can be tested directly.

whys.result: The default TCP congestion control is TcpCubic.
whys.guess: Different TCP congestion controls respond differently to loss and delay; a loss-insensitive or bandwidth-estimating control such as TcpBbr may keep TCP closer to the bottleneck capacity than Cubic.
whys.unseen: BBR's internal bandwidth and RTprop estimates, pacing rate, and probe behavior are not visible in the summary metrics.
whys.matters: If algorithm choice matters, tcp.type could give a larger TCP goodput without changing queue length.
whys.reason: All TCP choices can be compared at the default queue in one experiment.

whys.result: l1_util is already 1.0, UDP is 300 Mbps, and the UDP-loss constraint allows only a small increase in UDP loss.
whys.guess: The result may be hard-bounded by link capacity and the UDP flow: even eliminating TCP retransmissions and using the full allowed UDP loss may change TCP goodput by less than the 1% tolerance.
whys.unseen: Exact packet overhead, UDP bits actually sent on the link, and the capacity available to TCP payload after headers are not directly reported.
whys.matters: If this capacity-bound explanation is true, no allowed setting should make a meaningful difference, and the best recommendation may be the default.
whys.reason: The TCP-type and queue-length tests will show whether any setting can exceed the 1% tolerance.

answer.observations: E1 and C1/C2 show that no TCP type at queue 100 and no tested queue length with Cubic gives a feasible >1% TCP gain. The important unexplained pattern is that, for all saturated runs, udp_goodput_bps + tcp_goodput_bps is about 968.6 Mbps: Q4 and Q10 raise TCP goodput only by increasing UDP loss, while Q500 and Q1000 remove drops but do not raise TCP. BBR and Vegas underutilize the link. The next question is whether intermediate queue lengths, or TCP types at a short but feasible queue, can break this apparent UDP-loss ceiling.

rethink.because: Changing queue length changed Cubic drops from 2 to 12015, but TCP goodput stayed near 668-678 Mbps and total delivered payload stayed near 968.6 Mbps; reducing loss did not raise TCP goodput, so loss-induced backoff is not the limiting cause of a feasible gain.
Larger queues (500, 1000) removed drops but did not raise TCP goodput; smaller queues (4, 10) raised TCP only by causing UDP loss above 1%, so queue length did not give a feasible >1% gain.
At queue 100 no TCP type exceeded default by more than 1%; BBR and Vegas underutilized the link, while NewReno, LinuxReno, and Bic were within tolerance.

The sums udp_goodput_bps+tcp_goodput_bps are about 968.6 Mbps for all saturated TCP types and queue lengths, and TCP gains at Q4/Q10 are matched by UDP losses, indicating a capacity/UDP-loss ceiling rather than a setting that can improve TCP by >1%.

whys.result: For saturated runs, udp_goodput_bps+tcp_goodput_bps is about 968.6 Mbps, and Q4/Q10 TCP gains are offset by UDP losses.
whys.guess: The sender queue is a shared bottleneck with a fixed delivered-payload ceiling; queue length and TCP type mainly reallocate drops between UDP and TCP instead of increasing total delivered payload.
whys.unseen: Packet overhead, fixed UDP offered rate, and per-flow queue occupancy/drop timing are not in the summary metrics.
whys.matters: If UDP loss must stay <=1%, UDP delivered is at least about 297 Mbps, leaving TCP at most about 671.6 Mbps, less than 1% above default.
whys.reason: This explains why no tested setting improved and predicts a ceiling that intermediate queue lengths and TCP types should not break.

answer.observations: E2 and C3/C4 close the direct search: Cubic queue lengths 12-75 and non-Cubic TCP types at queue 30 all either keep tcp_goodput_bps <= 675.547 Mbps or violate udp_loss_frac <= 0.01. Across all saturated runs (Cubic/NewReno/LinuxReno/Bic at queues 4-1000), udp_goodput_bps + tcp_goodput_bps is about 968.5-968.64 Mbps. Q4 raises TCP to 677.57 Mbps only by causing UDP loss 3.02%; Q10 raises TCP to 672.35 Mbps with UDP loss 1.26%. BBR and Vegas keep UDP loss zero but leave l1_util at 0.733/0.845 and TCP far below the saturated runs. The remaining unexplained detail is exact packet overhead, but the measured total delivered-payload ceiling plus the UDP-loss constraint already bounds feasible TCP below the 1% improvement threshold.

report.limit: At the recommendation the result is limited by the fixed 1 Gbps link capacity and packet overhead, together with the UDP-loss constraint, not by TCP loss backoff. Saturated runs deliver about 968.6 Mbps of UDP+TCP payload. UDP is offered at about 300.003 Mbps payload, so udp_loss_frac <= 0.01 forces UDP delivered to be at least about 297.003 Mbps, leaving at most about 671.63 Mbps for TCP. The 1% improvement threshold over the default is 675.55 Mbps, so no feasible setting can exceed the default by a meaningful margin. Evidence: E0, E1, E2, C1, C2, C3, C4.
report.explanation: Default Cubic at queue 100 saturates the link and reaches the feasible ceiling. Queue length does not raise the ceiling: larger queues (500, 1000) remove drops but TCP remains about 668.6-669.8 Mbps; smaller queues can shift drops toward UDP, raising TCP only when UDP loss exceeds the allowed 1% (Q4) or still below the 1% threshold (Q10). TCP type matters only in that loss-based controls (Cubic, NewReno, LinuxReno, Bic) saturate and are equivalent within tolerance, while BBR and Vegas keep UDP loss zero but leave capacity unused (411.4 and 519.6 Mbps TCP). Therefore the best feasible setting is the simplest default. Among feasible queue lengths tested (12-1000), queue length is not a goodput knob; it only controls whether the UDP-loss constraint is met.
report.holds_when: UDP offered rate remains 300 Mbps, link rate remains 1 Gbps, packet sizes and overhead remain fixed, the queue is FIFO, TCP is always backlogged, and the UDP-loss constraint is 1%.
report.breaks_when: If the UDP-loss constraint were relaxed to about 3% or more, Q4 Cubic would give 677.6 Mbps; if UDP offered rate, packet overhead, or link rate changed so that the total delivered-payload ceiling rose above about 972.6 Mbps, a >1% feasible TCP gain could become possible; if TCP packetization changed, the ceiling would change.

claims.text: Saturated runs have a fixed total delivered-payload ceiling of about 968.6 Mbps.
With udp_loss_frac <= 0.01, UDP must deliver at least about 297.0 Mbps, so TCP cannot exceed about 671.6 Mbps, below the 1% threshold of 675.5 Mbps.
No tested Cubic queue length from 12 to 1000 packets gave a feasible TCP goodput more than 1% above default.
No tested non-Cubic TCP type gave a feasible TCP goodput more than 1% above default; BBR and Vegas underutilize the link.
Smaller queues can raise TCP only by reallocating drops to UDP, which violates the UDP-loss constraint when the TCP gain is large.
Default Cubic at queue 100 is best among feasible settings because it is within tolerance of all feasible near-max settings and is the simplest safe choice.

open_questions: Exact packet overhead was inferred from total delivered payload, not measured directly from headers.

I did not simulate every integer queue length or every TCP type at every queue length; the capacity ceiling makes a >1% feasible gain impossible under the fixed overhead, but direct exhaustive confirmation was not run.
The internal reason BBR and Vegas underutilize the link was not tested; it does not affect the maximum because they are far below the feasible ceiling.
